QF.id: Terminology in Equity and Debt Markets_26

question.text: Accrued interest on a bond refers to:

answer.text: The total interest earned over the bond's lifetime
Interest accumulated since the last coupon payment date up to the settlement date
The interest rate charged by the RBI on overnight lending

explanation.text: The Logic: Bonds pay coupons at discrete intervals (semi-annual, annual, etc.), but interest economically accrues every day the bond is held. "Accrued interest" is the portion of the next coupon that has been earned by the seller from the most recent coupon payment date up to the settlement date of a trade. When a bond is bought between coupon dates, the buyer pays the seller this accrued amount in addition to the negotiated price, so the seller is compensated for the days they held the bond during the current coupon period. The Trap: Total interest over the bond's lifetime is the sum of all coupons (and any discount/premium amortisation), not accrued interest. The RBI's overnight lending rate is a money-market policy rate, unrelated. Future interest until maturity is a forward-looking cash-flow stream, not the day-count accrual since the last coupon. Note: The specific definition of accrued interest as the amount running from the last coupon date to settlement is not stated on the cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst pages checked (pp.51, 65-66, 75, 151, 153, 173). The framing above reflects general industry/market-convention usage (and the related clean-price/dirty-price terminology) rather than the cited workbook chapter.
